---
title: "Set 13 — correspondence analysis"
subtitle: "After lecture 15 · 17 November · about 35 minutes"
---

Data: [`brands.csv`](../materials/brands.csv) — 2 356 respondent × brand ×
attribute associations. Build the contingency table with `table(brands$brand,
brands$attribute)`.

## 1 · Is there anything to analyse

Run `chisq.test` on the table. Report the statistic, the degrees of freedom and
the p-value.

Correspondence analysis decomposes exactly this statistic. What would it mean to
run CA on a table where the test came back at p = 0.4 — would the plot be empty,
or would it be misleading? Answer carefully: this is the trap.

## 2 · Inertia is chi-square in disguise

Fit `ca::ca(tab)`. Report total inertia and the percentage on the first two
dimensions.

Verify numerically that total inertia equals $\chi^2 / n$. Then say, in one
sentence, what "explaining 78% of the inertia" is explaining.

## 3 · Read the map, with discipline

Plot the symmetric map.

- Name the contrast each axis captures, in the language of the attributes
- Identify one brand that sits near the origin. What does that position mean, and
  why is "average" a better word than "unremarkable"?

## 4 · The distance you are not allowed to read

A student points at brand B and attribute *Reliable*, close together, and says
"B is reliable".

Explain what is wrong with that reading on a symmetric map, and what you *can*
legitimately say about B and *Reliable*. Then state what you would have to plot
instead to make the student's sentence defensible.

## 5 · One slide for the client

Produce a single figure with a one-line title that a brand manager could act on.
Nothing else — no table, no second panel.

Write the sentence you would say while showing it.

---

*This set checks: that CA is a decomposition of a test you already know, and
that reading a symmetric map row-to-column is the standard mistake.*
